screens.title: VM Stack Arithmetic: add, sub, neg, and comparisons
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a solid mental model of the VM’s stack arithmetic. The VM evaluates expressions by popping operands off a stack, performing an ALU operation, and pushing the result back. That simple execution model underlies add, sub, and neg, as well as the comparison commands eq, gt, and lt. You will see concrete assembly sequences that implement each command and learn why comparisons require subtraction plus a conditional jump. You will also explore practical translator responsibilities: maintaining SP in R A M[0], mapping push/pop to memory accesses, and generating unique labels for each comparison to avoid conflicts. Along the way we’ll connect these ideas to examples you can run in the Computer Simulator: a small addition program, a subtraction-and-negation pair, and a multi-step comparison test. By the end you’ll understand both the VM concept—pop, compute, push—and the low-level assembly patterns that realize it. Keep an eye out for a common misconception: comparisons don’t return 1 and 0; they push -1 for true and 0 for false, a choice that simplifies bitwise operations. Why does that choice help the translator? We’ll answer that and show how to test your generated assembly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter gives you four pragmatic skills you will carry into building a VM translator. First, you will implement the basic arithmetic VM commands add, sub and neg so you can evaluate numeric expressions on the stack. You will practice writing the assembly sequences that pop operands, compute, and push results. Second, you will implement the comparison commands eq, gt and lt, and learn to represent true as -1 and false as 0. You’ll see why that representation is useful for bitwise operations and how it maps to pushing a value onto the stack. Third, you will translate VM arithmetic commands into Hack assembly, including the exact sequence of memory and ALU operations required. This teaches code generation discipline: correct ordering, SP updates, and readable sequences. Fourth, you will understand how the VM uses the stack for expression evaluation, including SP management in R A M[0], push/pop semantics, and the stack’s growth from address 256. Each objective is paired with short practice tasks so you can test correctness in the Computer Simulator.

screens.title: Stack execution model
screens.narratorSegment: The VM evaluates expressions using a simple, consistent model: pop operands from the stack, perform an ALU operation, and push the result. This pop-compute-push cycle means every arithmetic or comparison command manipulates the top of the stack and updates SP appropriately. Concretely, SP is kept in R A M[0] and points to the next free slot; pushes write at R A M[SP] then increment SP, and pops decrement SP and then read R A M[SP]. The stack grows from address 256 upward. For example, push constant 3 writes 3 at R A M[256] if SP is 256, then sets SP to 257. When add runs, it expects two operands on top: x (below) and y (top). The command decrements SP twice to access both values, computes x+y in the ALU, stores the result at R A M[SP] and increments SP. A common misconception is to think the VM performs arithmetic on named variables; instead it always operates on stack values and uses SP as the only pointer. Understanding this model helps you reason about ordering: the left operand is the value below the top; the right operand is the top. That ordering matters for subtraction and comparisons. Ask yourself: given a sequence of pushes and pops, can you predict the stack contents after each operation?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Stack-based execution: pop operands, perform ALU op, push result; SP in RAM[0] points to next free slot.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Stack Execution Model
Definition

Pop, compute, push

SP in RAM[0] always points at the next free location. Push writes then increments. Pop decrements then reads.

Push (example)
push constant 3: RAM[SP] = 3; SP = SP + 1. If SP starts at 256, 3 ends up at RAM[256].
Pop (behavior)
A pop first decrements SP, then reads from RAM[SP]. That guarantees the top value is consumed and SP always points to next free slot.
Common misconception
Do not assume operations use named registers. The VM always reads from the stack via SP; operand ordering depends on stack positions.
Process Flow

Example: add

Stack before: [..., x, y] Stack after: [..., x+y] SP manipulation summary: 1. AM = M - 1 -> address y 2. D = M -> D = y 3. AM = M - 1 -> address x 4. D = D + M -> D = x + y 5. M = D -> store result 6. M = M + 1 -> increment SP
Concrete example
push constant 3; push constant 5; add → stack holds 8 at top.
Key takeaway
Keep SP updates paired with memory accesses to prevent off-by-one stack errors.
Check your understanding
  • When add executes, which value is treated as x and which as y?
  • Why must pop decrement SP before reading RAM[SP]?

screens.title: add — assembly implementation
screens.narratorSegment: The add command pops two values and pushes their sum. The assembly sequence is deterministic and follows a pattern that both a translator and a human can memorize. The translator first decrements SP and stores the top value into D. Then it decrements SP again to land on the second operand and adds D to M. Finally it stores the result at the same address and increments SP. This ordering guarantees that the value originally below the top is treated as the left operand and the top as the right. A concrete example: if the stack holds 3 and 5, running add produces 8. A common mistake is to increment or decrement SP in the wrong order, which either loses a value or overwrites the wrong cell. The code block on the slide shows the standard implementation you should generate for every add; practice by replacing add with sub and neg and observe how small changes produce the expected arithmetic differences. Remember: the assembly sequence must preserve SP invariants so downstream commands see a well-formed stack. add — assembly implementation means for add: decrement sp twice, d = y, d = d + m, store and increment sp. preserve operand ordering and sp invariants.. In practical terms, exact instruction sequence that implements vm add. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › add Implementation
Code Walkthrough

Standard add sequence

<!-- Assembly implementation for add --> @SP AM=M-1 // SP = SP - 1, A = SP (point to y) D=M // D = y @SP AM=M-1 // SP = SP - 1, A = SP (point to x) D=D+M // D = x + y M=D // Push result @SP M=M+1 // SP = SP + 1
Concrete example

If the stack contains [..., 3, 5], after add it contains [..., 8]. Try this sequence in the simulator to confirm SP ends at the expected value and no data is lost.

Common mistake

If you increment SP before storing the result you will write to the wrong cell and the next command will use an incorrect top-of-stack value. Keep the store-before-increment order.

Supporting cards
Example card
push constant 3; push constant 5; add → 8 on stack.
Why order matters
x is the value below the top; y is the top. For subtraction, x - y must respect that order.
Key takeaway
Memorize the SP decrement, compute, store, increment pattern for binary arithmetic commands.

screens.title: sub and neg — small variations
screens.narratorSegment: Subtraction and negation are small but important variations on the add pattern. For sub, the translator follows the same SP manipulations as add, but the ALU operation changes: we compute x - y instead of x + y. Practically that means after popping y into D and stepping to x, you perform D=M-D or D=M-D depending on the exact register convention so D ends up with x - y. The rest of the sequence—store and increment SP—remains identical. For neg, the operation is unary: it only looks at the top value. Negation is implemented by addressing SP-1 and replacing M with -M; there is no double pop. A concrete example: push constant 10; push constant 7; sub produces 3; then neg produces -3. A frequent misconception is to attempt to treat neg like a binary operation; remember that neg touches only the top value and must not change SP. When you implement these, test both single-operand and two-operand sequences to ensure SP and memory remain well-formed. sub and neg — small variations means sub changes the alu op to x-y; neg is unary and in-place on top of stack without changing sp.. In practical terms, how subtraction and negation differ from add. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › sub & neg
Code Walkthrough

sub (binary) and neg (unary)

<!-- sub implementation (pattern like add, ALU change) --> @SP AM=M-1 // SP = SP - 1, A = SP (point to y) D=M // D = y @SP AM=M-1 // SP = SP - 1, A = SP (point to x) D=M-D // D = x - y M=D // Push result @SP M=M+1 // SP = SP + 1 <!-- neg implementation (unary) --> @SP A=M-1 // A = top of stack M=-M // Negate top value
Concrete example

push constant 10; push constant 7; sub → 3 on stack. Then neg → -3 in place of 3. SP unchanged after neg.

Pitfall

Treating neg as a pop-compute-push will incorrectly adjust SP. Implement neg by directly negating RAM[SP-1].

Supporting cards
Unary vs binary
Unary commands operate on one stack element and often do not change SP; binary commands consume two elements and push one.
Testing tip
After implementing neg, run a sequence combining binary and unary ops to ensure SP is consistent at each step.
Key takeaway
Small ALU changes map to different VM commands; keep SP rules consistent across implementations.

screens.title: eq, gt, lt — boolean representation
screens.narratorSegment: Comparisons differ from arithmetic because the Hack platform lacks a native compare instruction. The translator therefore computes x - y and uses conditional jumps to push either -1 for true or 0 for false. The VM convention uses -1 for true because, in two's complement, -1 is all ones, which plays nicely with bitwise operations. For example, after computing D = x - y, an eq command tests D; if D equals zero the translator jumps to a label that writes -1 into R A M[SP], otherwise it writes 0. Afterward SP increments. A concrete example: push constant 5; push constant 3; gt will push -1 because 5 > 3. A common misconception is to expect 1 for true; if you generate 1 instead of -1 some bitwise combinations will behave incorrectly. The translator must therefore explicitly emit M=-1 for true and M=0 for false. Practice reading simulated stack traces to confirm that the top-of-stack holds -1 or 0 after each comparison. eq, gt, lt — boolean representation means comparisons push -1 for true and 0 for false; use subtraction and conditional jumps to decide which value to push.. In practical terms, how comparisons push -1 for true and 0 for false. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Comparisons & Booleans
Comparison semantics

eq, gt, lt push boolean values

Compute x - y and use the ALU’s result to decide between -1 (true) and 0 (false). The translator emits jump logic that writes the chosen value and then increments SP.

Concrete example
push constant 5; push constant 3; gt → stack top is -1 (true) because 5 > 3.
Why -1?
-1 is all ones in two's complement; it composes naturally with bitwise operations and can be produced directly by the ALU.
Misconception
Do not use 1 for true. Some operations expect a mask of all ones to propagate truth in bitwise logic.
Example sequence
push constant 5
push constant 3
gt  // pushes -1
push constant 5
push constant 5
eq  // pushes -1
Key takeaway
Always ensure the translator writes -1 or 0 explicitly in your generated assembly. When testing, check the simulator’s RAM at the stack address to verify the exact bit pattern.

screens.title: Implementing eq with labels and jumps
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing eq demonstrates several translator responsibilities in one sequence: compute x - y, test the result, conditionally write -1 or 0, and increment SP. Because labels are used for the true and end destinations, the translator must create unique labels per comparison. A typical generated snippet computes D = x - y, then jumps to EQ_TRUE_N if D equals zero; otherwise it falls through to writing 0 and then jumps to EQ_END_N. Then the EQ_TRUE_N label writes -1 and continues to EQ_END_N where SP is incremented. The translator keeps a global counter and appends it to label names like EQ_TRUE_1 and EQ_END_1. If labels were reused, the assembler would either reject duplicates or cause ambiguous jumps. A concrete example: two separate eq commands in a program must use different numeric suffixes. When you implement eq, verify that each invocation increments the counter. This is a small code-generation discipline that prevents subtle runtime faults and assembly errors. Implementing eq with labels and jumps means comparisons require unique labels per invocation; maintain a global counter in the translator to generate eq_true_1, eq_end_1, etc.. In practical terms, assembly pattern and the need for unique labels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › eq Implementation
Assembly Example
// Compute x - y @SP AM=M-1 D=M @SP AM=M-1 D=M-D // D = x - y // If D == 0, jump to EQ_TRUE @EQ_TRUE_1 D;JEQ // Not equal: push 0 @SP A=M M=0 @EQ_END_1 0;JMP (EQ_TRUE_1) @SP A=M M=-1 // Push -1 (true) (EQ_END_1) @SP M=M+1
Why unique labels matter

Each eq generates its own EQ_TRUE_n and EQ_END_n so jumps refer to unambiguous targets. A global counter avoids duplicate label definitions and ambiguous jump destinations.

Testing tip

Generate multiple comparisons in a single .asm and inspect label names. Ensure counters increment for each eq, gt, or lt.

Supporting cards
Label pattern
Use a counter: EQ_TRUE_1, EQ_END_1, then EQ_TRUE_2, EQ_END_2, etc.
Common failure
Reusing labels creates assembler errors or wrong control flow. Always increment the counter for each comparison.
Key takeaway
Label generation is a translator concern as much as the instruction sequence itself.

screens.title: Push and Pop mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: Push and pop are the primitive memory operations the translator emits for many commands. Push stores a value at R A M[SP] then increments SP. Pop decrements SP and reads R A M[SP]. This careful ordering ensures SP always points to the next free cell and that no value is accidentally overwritten. For instance, a push constant v sequence typically loads the constant into D, writes D to R A M[SP], and finally increments SP. A pop to a segment will decrement SP, set A to R A M[SP], then store the top value into the target segment address. Developers often make off-by-one errors by reversing increment and store actions. To avoid this, reason in terms of the SP invariant: after any command completes, SP must again point to the next free location. A practical test is to push several constants and then pop them into a temporary variable, confirming the retrieved values match the push order. This test reveals whether your translator maintains the correct order and pointer semantics. Push and Pop mechanics means after each command, sp must point to the next free stack address. push: write then increment. pop: decrement then read.. In practical terms, precise sequences for writing and reading the stack. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Push and pop are the primitive memory operations the translator emits for many commands. Push stores a value at R A M[SP] then increments SP. Pop decrements SP and reads R A M[SP]. This careful ordering ensures SP always points to the next free cell and that no value is accidentally overwritten. For instance, a push constant v sequence typically loads the constant into D, writes D to R A M[SP], and finally increments SP. A pop to a segment will decrement SP, set A to R A M[SP], then store the top value into the target segment address. Developers often make off-by-one errors by reversing increment and store actions. To avoid this, reason in terms of the SP invariant: after any command completes, SP must again point to the next free location. A practical test is to push several constants and then pop them into a temporary variable, confirming the retrieved values match the push order. This test reveals whether your translator maintains the correct order and pointer semantics. Push and Pop mechanics means after each command, sp must point to the next free stack address. push: write then increment. pop: decrement then read.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Push & Pop mechanics
Process

Push and pop sequences

Push: D contains value, store at RAM[SP], then SP = SP + 1. Pop: SP = SP - 1, then read RAM[SP]. When popping into a segment, compute the target address first, then overwrite it with the popped value. Keeping these orders prevents accidental overwrite and maintains the SP invariant for subsequent operations.
Concrete example
push constant 3; push constant 5; pop temp 0 → temp 0 receives 5; the stack top becomes 3.
Bug pattern
Incrementing SP before writing during push will leave a zero at the old top and write the value to the next slot, shifting stack contents unexpectedly.
Cards
Push pattern
D = value; @SP; A=M; M=D; @SP; M=M+1
Pop pattern
@SP; AM=M-1; D=M; // D now has popped value
Key takeaway
Always reason about where SP points before and after each stack operation to avoid off-by-one errors.

screens.title: The VM translator as a code generator
screens.narratorSegment: The VM translator is a code generator: it reads VM commands and emits sequences of Hack assembly that implement them. Its responsibilities include: correctly mapping each VM command to its assembly pattern; maintaining SP in R A M[0] so the produced assembly uses the correct stack pointer; generating unique labels for comparisons and any control flow; and mapping VM memory segments to hardware addresses. screens.title: Label collisions and assembler errors
screens.narratorSegment: Label collisions are a frequent, avoidable source of errors in the generated assembly. If multiple comparison commands emit the same label names, the assembler will either reject the output or produce ambiguous jump targets. Consider two eq commands that both generate EQ_TRUE and EQ_END without numeric suffixes. The assembler may see duplicate label definitions or the first label may satisfy all jumps, causing incorrect control flow. The right remedy is simple: maintain a global counter inside the translator that increments each time a comparison is translated. Append this counter to both the true and end labels. For example, EQ_TRUE_1 / EQ_END_1 for the first comparison, then EQ_TRUE_2 / EQ_END_2 for the next. A practical test is to compile a. vm file with several comparisons and search the. asm for duplicate label names. If duplicates exist, incrementing the counter or centralizing label generation will fix the problem. This discipline is a small but essential part of making a reliable code generator. Label collisions and assembler errors means duplicate labels cause assembly failures or wrong jumps. use a monotonically increasing counter to create unique label names per comparison.. Why unique labels matter

If the translator emits identical label names for multiple comparisons, either the assembler will report duplicate definitions or control flow will jump to the wrong target. Ambiguous jumps can result in incorrect boolean values on the stack or runtime faults.

Detect duplicates by searching the generated .asm for repeated label names.
Fix by centralizing label generation and incrementing a counter each time you emit comparison code.
Test with multiple comparisons in one file to ensure label suffixes increase.
Cards
Symptom: assembler reports duplicate label definition or wrong jumps occur.
Resolution: maintain a global counter and append it to labels used by comparisons.
Key takeaway: label generation is a core translator responsibility to ensure correct control flow.

screens.title: Why a stack is natural for expression evaluation
screens.narratorSegment: A stack is a natural data structure for expression evaluation because it mirrors the nested structure of computations and supports last-in, first-out ordering for operands. When an expression is written in postfix or when operations are nested, pushing operands and then popping them to apply operators matches the natural evaluation order. Practically, the stack simplifies the translator design: each VM command requires only local knowledge of the top elements and SP to perform its work, without needing complex register allocation. The stack representation also maps cleanly to subexpression evaluation during function calls and expression trees. One practical benefit is simplicity: generating code for a stack-based VM requires fewer global decisions than register allocation. A common misconception is that stacks are inefficient; while they can impose more memory accesses, they simplify correctness and translator complexity, which matters in the early stages of a system’s construction. Reflect: given the VM command set, how would expression evaluation change if the VM used registers instead of a stack? Why a stack is natural for expression evaluation means stacks match nested evaluation and keep the translator simple: local operations on sp make code generation straightforward.. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a solid mental model of the VM’s stack arithmetic. The VM evaluates expressions by popping operands off a stack, performing an ALU operation, and pushing the result back. That simple execution model underlies add, sub, and neg, as well as the comparison commands eq, gt, and lt. You will see concrete assembly sequences that implement each command and learn why comparisons require subtraction plus a conditional jump. You will also explore practical translator responsibilities: maintaining SP in R A M[0], mapping push/pop to memory accesses, and generating unique labels for each comparison to avoid conflicts. Along the way we’ll connect these ideas to examples you can run in the Computer Simulator: a small addition program, a subtraction-and-negation pair, and a multi-step comparison test. By the end you’ll understand both the VM concept—pop, compute, push—and the low-level assembly patterns that realize it. Keep an eye out for a common misconception: comparisons don’t return 1 and 0; they push -1 for true and 0 for false, a choice that simplifies bitwise operations. Why does that choice help the translator? We’ll answer that and show how to test your generated assembly.

This chapter gives you four pragmatic skills you will carry into building a VM translator. First, you will implement the basic arithmetic VM commands add, sub and neg so you can evaluate numeric expressions on the stack. You will practice writing the assembly sequences that pop operands, compute, and push results. Second, you will implement the comparison commands eq, gt and lt, and learn to represent true as -1 and false as 0. You’ll see why that representation is useful for bitwise operations and how it maps to pushing a value onto the stack. Third, you will translate VM arithmetic commands into Hack assembly, including the exact sequence of memory and ALU operations required. This teaches code generation discipline: correct ordering, SP updates, and readable sequences. Fourth, you will understand how the VM uses the stack for expression evaluation, including SP management in R A M[0], push/pop semantics, and the stack’s growth from address 256. Each objective is paired with short practice tasks so you can test correctness in the Computer Simulator.

Beyond implementation, this chapter prepares you to test and harden a VM translator. You will practice generating unique labels for comparisons so each eq, gt, or lt compiles to a distinct jump target. This prevents label collisions that would break assembly. You will also test how the translator encodes true as -1 and false as 0, and see why that choice is convenient for bitwise operations. Another objective is to exercise push and pop for constants and verify the final stack contents in the Computer Simulator. Finally, you will learn how to increment a global comparison counter inside your translator to avoid duplicate labels and how to verify your translator with small programs: simple addition, subtraction-then-negation, and a two-part comparison test. These practice objectives turn conceptual knowledge into repeatable translator behaviors you can verify programmatically.

The VM evaluates expressions using a simple, consistent model: pop operands from the stack, perform an ALU operation, and push the result. This pop-compute-push cycle means every arithmetic or comparison command manipulates the top of the stack and updates SP appropriately. Concretely, SP is kept in R A M[0] and points to the next free slot; pushes write at R A M[SP] then increment SP, and pops decrement SP and then read R A M[SP]. The stack grows from address 256 upward. For example, push constant 3 writes 3 at R A M[256] if SP is 256, then sets SP to 257. When add runs, it expects two operands on top: x (below) and y (top). The command decrements SP twice to access both values, computes x+y in the ALU, stores the result at R A M[SP] and increments SP. A common misconception is to think the VM performs arithmetic on named variables; instead it always operates on stack values and uses SP as the only pointer. Understanding this model helps you reason about ordering: the left operand is the value below the top; the right operand is the top. That ordering matters for subtraction and comparisons. Ask yourself: given a sequence of pushes and pops, can you predict the stack contents after each operation?

The add command pops two values and pushes their sum. The assembly sequence is deterministic and follows a pattern that both a translator and a human can memorize. The translator first decrements SP and stores the top value into D. Then it decrements SP again to land on the second operand and adds D to M. Finally it stores the result at the same address and increments SP. This ordering guarantees that the value originally below the top is treated as the left operand and the top as the right. A concrete example: if the stack holds 3 and 5, running add produces 8. A common mistake is to increment or decrement SP in the wrong order, which either loses a value or overwrites the wrong cell. The code block on the slide shows the standard implementation you should generate for every add; practice by replacing add with sub and neg and observe how small changes produce the expected arithmetic differences. Remember: the assembly sequence must preserve SP invariants so downstream commands see a well-formed stack. add — assembly implementation means for add: decrement sp twice, d = y, d = d + m, store and increment sp. preserve operand ordering and sp invariants.. In practical terms, exact instruction sequence that implements vm add. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Subtraction and negation are small but important variations on the add pattern. For sub, the translator follows the same SP manipulations as add, but the ALU operation changes: we compute x - y instead of x + y. Practically that means after popping y into D and stepping to x, you perform D=M-D or D=M-D depending on the exact register convention so D ends up with x - y. The rest of the sequence—store and increment SP—remains identical. For neg, the operation is unary: it only looks at the top value. Negation is implemented by addressing SP-1 and replacing M with -M; there is no double pop. A concrete example: push constant 10; push constant 7; sub produces 3; then neg produces -3. A frequent misconception is to attempt to treat neg like a binary operation; remember that neg touches only the top value and must not change SP. When you implement these, test both single-operand and two-operand sequences to ensure SP and memory remain well-formed. sub and neg — small variations means sub changes the alu op to x-y; neg is unary and in-place on top of stack without changing sp.. In practical terms, how subtraction and negation differ from add. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparisons differ from arithmetic because the Hack platform lacks a native compare instruction. The translator therefore computes x - y and uses conditional jumps to push either -1 for true or 0 for false. The VM convention uses -1 for true because, in two's complement, -1 is all ones, which plays nicely with bitwise operations. For example, after computing D = x - y, an eq command tests D; if D equals zero the translator jumps to a label that writes -1 into R A M[SP], otherwise it writes 0. Afterward SP increments. A concrete example: push constant 5; push constant 3; gt will push -1 because 5 > 3. A common misconception is to expect 1 for true; if you generate 1 instead of -1 some bitwise combinations will behave incorrectly. The translator must therefore explicitly emit M=-1 for true and M=0 for false. Practice reading simulated stack traces to confirm that the top-of-stack holds -1 or 0 after each comparison. eq, gt, lt — boolean representation means comparisons push -1 for true and 0 for false; use subtraction and conditional jumps to decide which value to push.. In practical terms, how comparisons push -1 for true and 0 for false. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Implementing eq demonstrates several translator responsibilities in one sequence: compute x - y, test the result, conditionally write -1 or 0, and increment SP. Because labels are used for the true and end destinations, the translator must create unique labels per comparison. A typical generated snippet computes D = x - y, then jumps to EQ_TRUE_N if D equals zero; otherwise it falls through to writing 0 and then jumps to EQ_END_N. Then the EQ_TRUE_N label writes -1 and continues to EQ_END_N where SP is incremented. The translator keeps a global counter and appends it to label names like EQ_TRUE_1 and EQ_END_1. If labels were reused, the assembler would either reject duplicates or cause ambiguous jumps. A concrete example: two separate eq commands in a program must use different numeric suffixes. When you implement eq, verify that each invocation increments the counter. This is a small code-generation discipline that prevents subtle runtime faults and assembly errors. Implementing eq with labels and jumps means comparisons require unique labels per invocation; maintain a global counter in the translator to generate eq_true_1, eq_end_1, etc.. Push and pop are the primitive memory operations the translator emits for many commands. Push stores a value at R A M[SP] then increments SP. Pop decrements SP and reads R A M[SP]. This careful ordering ensures SP always points to the next free cell and that no value is accidentally overwritten. For instance, a push constant v sequence typically loads the constant into D, writes D to R A M[SP], and finally increments SP. A pop to a segment will decrement SP, set A to R A M[SP], then store the top value into the target segment address. Developers often make off-by-one errors by reversing increment and store actions. To avoid this, reason in terms of the SP invariant: after any command completes, SP must again point to the next free location. A practical test is to push several constants and then pop them into a temporary variable, confirming the retrieved values match the push order. This test reveals whether your translator maintains the correct order and pointer semantics. The VM translator is a code generator: it reads VM commands and emits sequences of Hack assembly that implement them. Its responsibilities include: correctly mapping each VM command to its assembly pattern; maintaining SP in R A M[0] so the produced assembly uses the correct stack pointer; generating unique labels for comparisons and any control flow; and mapping VM memory segments to hardware addresses. For arithmetic commands, the translator emits the deterministic sequences we studied earlier. For push and pop, it emits address computation and memory reads/writes. For comparisons, it emits subtraction, conditional jumps, the -1/0 writes, and SP increments. A translator must also be careful to preserve program ordering and to avoid side effects between generated snippets. A practical approach is to implement the arithmetic command generator as small functions that return sequences of assembly lines, and to centralize label generation in a single counter so every comparison gets a fresh suffix. This modular design produces readable. asm and simplifies debugging. Label collisions are a frequent, avoidable source of errors in the generated assembly. If multiple comparison commands emit the same label names, the assembler will either reject the output or produce ambiguous jump targets. Consider two eq commands that both generate EQ_TRUE and EQ_END without numeric suffixes. The assembler may see duplicate label definitions or the first label may satisfy all jumps, causing incorrect control flow. The right remedy is simple: maintain a global counter inside the translator that increments each time a comparison is translated. Append this counter to both the true and end labels. For example, EQ_TRUE_1 / EQ_END_1 for the first comparison, then EQ_TRUE_2 / EQ_END_2 for the next. A practical test is to compile a. vm file with several comparisons and search the. asm for duplicate label names. If duplicates exist, incrementing the counter or centralizing label generation will fix the problem. This discipline is a small but essential part of making a reliable code generator. A stack is a natural data structure for expression evaluation because it mirrors the nested structure of computations and supports last-in, first-out ordering for operands. When an expression is written in postfix or when operations are nested, pushing operands and then popping them to apply operators matches the natural evaluation order. Practically, the stack simplifies the translator design: each VM command requires only local knowledge of the top elements and SP to perform its work, without needing complex register allocation. The stack representation also maps cleanly to subexpression evaluation during function calls and expression trees. One practical benefit is simplicity: generating code for a stack-based VM requires fewer global decisions than register allocation. A common misconception is that stacks are inefficient; while they can impose more memory accesses, they simplify correctness and translator complexity, which matters in the early stages of a system’s construction. These are the core ideas to remember. The VM operates by popping operands off a stack, performing an ALU operation, and pushing the result. The arithmetic commands add, sub and neg map to small, deterministic assembly sequences that update SP and preserve operand order. Comparisons use subtraction plus jumps and must push -1 for true and 0 for false. The translator must also generate unique labels for comparisons to avoid assembler errors. Finally, SP lives in R A M[0], points to the next free slot, and push/pop semantics must maintain that invariant. Keep these points in mind as you implement and test your translator.
